title: The Wedding Feast and the Trap Questions
summary: Jesus tells a parable of a king whose invited guests refuse his son's wedding banquet and kill his messengers, so the hall is filled with people from the roads, though one guest without wedding clothes is thrown out. Then three groups test him in turn: Pharisees and Herodians on paying taxes to Caesar, Sadducees on the resurrection, and an expert in the law on the greatest commandment. Jesus answers each, and then asks his own question about how the Christ can be both David's son and David's Lord, which silences them all.
story:
This is still the day of debate in the temple courts during Jesus' last week in Jerusalem, often reckoned as the Tuesday. In chapter 21 the chief priests and elders challenged his authority (21:23), and he answered with three parables of judgment: the two sons (21:28-32), the tenants (21:33-44), and now the wedding banquet. The leaders understood that he was speaking about them and wanted to arrest him, but they feared the crowds, who held him to be a prophet (21:45-46). So they change tactics. Instead of confronting him, they try to trap him with questions designed to discredit him before the people or expose him to Rome.

Matthew follows Mark's order for the questions (Mark 12:13-37) but shapes them to his own ends. The questioner about the great commandment comes to test Jesus rather than, as in Mark, to agree with him, and the sentence that no one dared to question him any further is moved to the very end, after Jesus has asked his own question about David's son (verse 46). The effect is a clean sweep: every party in Jerusalem tries, and every party falls silent. Having silenced his opponents, Jesus will turn in chapter 23 to warn the crowds and his disciples about the scribes and Pharisees and pronounce his woes, the last public teaching in Matthew's Gospel.
historical:
The tax question sat on a live wire. When Herod's son Archelaus was deposed in AD 6 and Judea came under direct Roman rule, the legate of Syria, Quirinius, took a census to assess the new province for tribute (Josephus, Antiquities 18.1-10). Judas the Galilean led a revolt against it, teaching that to pay tribute to Rome was to accept mortal masters in place of God (Jewish War 2.118; Acts 5:37), and Josephus traces the later revolutionary movements to his teaching. Matthew calls the tax kēnsos, a loanword from the Latin census, and the coin ‘the coin used for the tax’. The question ‘Is it lawful?’ asks whether the Law of Moses permits paying it at all. A yes would anger a crowd that resented Rome; a no could be reported to the governor as sedition, the very charge that Luke says was later brought to Pilate (Luke 23:2).

The coin was a silver denarius, roughly a laborer's daily wage (20:2). The common denarius of Tiberius (emperor AD 14 to 37) bore his laureate head and the legend TI CAESAR DIVI AVG F AVGVSTVS, ‘Tiberius Caesar Augustus, son of the divine Augustus’, and on the reverse a seated female figure with the title PONTIF MAXIM, ‘high priest’. The bronze coins the Roman prefects minted in Judea carried no portrait of the emperor, so Jesus has to ask for a denarius, and his questioners can produce one on the spot. The Pharisees send their own disciples with the Herodians, supporters of the Herod family whose power rested on Rome, an unlikely alliance that Mark records forming in Galilee (Mark 3:6).

The Sadducees were a party of the priestly and lay aristocracy, closely tied to the temple leadership. Josephus says they held that the soul perishes with the body and that they rejected the traditions of the fathers that the Pharisees kept, accepting only what was written (Antiquities 13.297, 18.16-17; Jewish War 2.164-165), and Acts 23:8 adds that they denied the resurrection, angels, and spirits. Later church writers such as Origen (Against Celsus 1.49) and Hippolytus said they accepted only the five books of Moses; scholars debate whether that is accurate or a misunderstanding of their rejection of the oral tradition, but it would explain why Jesus answers them from Exodus. A later rabbinic legend traces their origin to Zadok, a disciple of Antigonus of Sokho, who took his teacher's saying about serving God without thought of reward as a denial of reward after death (Avot de-Rabbi Natan A 5). The Sadducees disappear from history with the temple in AD 70.

One detail in the parable has a history of its own. The king sends his troops to destroy the murderers and burn their city (verse 7), which is more than a wedding story needs. Many scholars, among them W. D. Davies and Dale Allison and Ulrich Luz, read it as looking back on AD 70, when Titus's soldiers burned the temple and then the lower city (Josephus, Jewish War 6.249-266, 6.353-355), and they use it to date Matthew after that year. Others, following Karl Heinrich Rengstorf's essay on the city of murderers (1960), note that the burning of a rebel city was stock language for a king's punitive campaign (compare Judges 1:8 and the Babylonian burning of Jerusalem in 2 Kings 25:9), so the verse need not have been written after the event. Either way, Matthew's first readers could hardly have heard it without thinking of Jerusalem's fall.

The question about David's son drew on a widespread hope. The Psalms of Solomon, written in the first century BC, pray for God to raise up the son of David to rule Israel and purge Jerusalem of Gentiles (Psalms of Solomon 17:21-25), and a scroll from Qumran reads God's promise to David in 2 Samuel 7 as a promise of the Branch of David who will arise at the end of days (4Q174, the Florilegium). Jesus' questioners answer at once, ‘David's’; what they cannot explain is the psalm.
cultural:
A wedding feast given by a king for his son was the grandest occasion a royal house could host, and refusing it was political as well as personal. Invitations came in two stages: a first invitation, then a summons by servants when the meal was ready, as the king's servants came to bring Haman to Esther's banquet (Esther 6:14). The king's message in verse 4 names his ‘dinner’ (ariston, usually the first main meal of the day, which here opens days of feasting) and his oxen and fattened cattle already slaughtered, so the refusal comes when the meat is on the fire. To accept an invitation and then ignore the summons was an insult; to seize and kill the messengers was rebellion. Jewish hope pictured the age to come as a banquet on God's mountain (Isaiah 25:6-8), so Jesus' hearers would take the feast as a picture of the kingdom. ‘The crossroads’ (verse 9) renders a phrase for the places where city streets run out into the country roads, where travelers, laborers, and beggars could be found.

Guests were expected to come washed and in clean or festive clothing, and a guest who came in soiled everyday clothes dishonored his host. Two Old Testament passages sit close to the scene. Zephaniah 1:7-8 pictures the day of the LORD as a sacrifice for which God has consecrated his guests, and then says he will punish those clothed in foreign attire. When Jehu gathered the worshipers of Baal, he had vestments brought out from the wardrobe for them (2 Kings 10:22), which some interpreters cite as a custom of the host supplying garments, though there is no clear evidence that wedding hosts did so. A rabbinic parable attributed to Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai (b. Shabbat 153a) is the closest parallel: a king invited his servants to a banquet without fixing the hour; the wise dressed and waited at the palace door, the foolish went about their work, and when the summons came suddenly the dressed were seated and the soiled were made to stand and watch. The rabbis read it as a call to repent every day, in the light of Ecclesiastes 9:8, which bids one's garments be always white. The punishment in verse 13 uses Matthew's recurring images of judgment, the outer darkness (8:12, 25:30) and weeping and gnashing of teeth (six times in Matthew), and binding hand and foot recalls 1 Enoch 10:4, where the rebel angel Azazel is bound hand and foot and cast into darkness.

The Sadducees' case rests on levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5-10): if a man died childless, his brother was to marry the widow, and the first son counted as the dead man's, so that his name and inheritance would continue. Matthew's verb for the brother marrying her, epigambreuō, is the one the Greek Old Testament uses when Judah tells Onan to do his duty to Tamar (Genesis 38:8). Their seven brothers may parody two stories they knew, Sarah in Tobit, who lost seven husbands (Tobit 3:8), and the seven brothers of 2 Maccabees 7, who died under Antiochus IV confessing that God would raise them.

The question about the greatest commandment was a real one among Jewish teachers. A tradition in the Babylonian Talmud (b. Makkot 23b-24a) has Rabbi Simlai count 613 commandments given to Moses, then describe David reducing them to eleven (Psalm 15), Isaiah to six, Micah to three, and Habakkuk to one, that the righteous shall live by faith (Habakkuk 2:4). Hillel summarized the Torah for a Gentile with the negative golden rule (b. Shabbat 31a), Rabbi Akiva called ‘love your neighbor as yourself’ a great principle of the Torah (Sifra on Leviticus 19:18), and Philo named piety toward God and justice and kindness toward people as the two chief heads of all the laws (Special Laws 2.63). The Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs already join love of the Lord and of the neighbor (Testament of Issachar 5:2; Testament of Dan 5:3). The Shema, from Deuteronomy 6:4-9, was recited morning and evening (m. Berakhot 1:1-2) and written in the tefillin bound on arm and forehead. Jesus' verb in verse 40, ‘hang’, has a rabbinic echo: the Mishnah says the laws of the Sabbath, festal offerings, and sacrilege are like mountains hanging by a hair, having little Scripture and many rules (m. Hagigah 1:8). Jesus says the reverse of the whole Law and the Prophets: everything hangs on two great commands.
literary:
The chapter has two parts: a parable that completes the trilogy begun at 21:28, and four controversy exchanges. The three parables share servants or sons, a refusal, and a judgment, and each is sharper than the last. This one is more openly allegorical than Luke's great banquet (Luke 14:15-24): the host is a king, the feast is for his son, the servants are sent twice and some are killed, the king's troops burn the murderers' city, and the new guests are gathered ‘both evil and good’. That last phrase ties the parable to Matthew's picture of a mixed community until the judgment, the wheat and the weeds and the net full of good and bad fish (13:24-30, 13:47-50). So the parable turns in its final scene. The first half is a warning to those who refuse; the second, verses 11 to 14, is a warning to those who accept. Many commentators think verses 11 to 13 were once a separate story that Matthew joined to the banquet parable, and the seam shows in the sudden move from a hall filled by servants to one guest singled out by the king.

Small repetitions bind the chapter. The king greets the underdressed guest as ‘Friend’ (hetaire), a word only Matthew uses, and always with an edge: for the grumbling laborer (20:13) and for Judas at the arrest (26:50). The guest ‘was speechless’, literally was muzzled (ephimōthē), and the same verb returns in verse 34, when Jesus has ‘silenced’ the Sadducees. The Pharisees' disciples open with flattery that happens to be true: Jesus is honest, teaches the way of God, and does not look at the face, an Old Testament idiom for partiality (Leviticus 19:15). Matthew twice calls the questions a testing (peirazō, verses 18 and 35), the verb used of the devil in the wilderness (4:1) and of Pharisees and Sadducees demanding a sign (16:1). Jesus answers them with Scripture, as he answered the tempter.

The controversy section builds to a reversal. Three groups ask three questions, one political, one doctrinal, one about the Law, and then Jesus asks, in the same form Matthew uses elsewhere, ‘What do you think?’ (verse 42; compare verse 17, 18:12, 21:28). The chapter that began with guests who would not come ends with questioners who dare not ask (verse 46). Matthew also frames the exchanges with crowds: they are astonished at his teaching (verse 33), as they were at the end of the Sermon on the Mount (7:28), and the reader is invited to be astonished with them.

outline.t: The parable of the wedding banquet

doctrines.note: The kingdom is a wedding feast a king gives for his son, and the invitation goes out to the roads once the first guests refuse. Entry is by the king's invitation, not by merit, since the new guests are gathered ‘both evil and good’ (verse 10). Yet the guest without wedding clothes shows that the kingdom's welcome is not indifference: the one who comes is expected to come changed, and the king himself inspects the hall.

Jesus refuses both revolt and idolatry. The coin bearing Caesar's image may be given back to Caesar, since rulers have a real, limited claim, but the things of God belong to God, and human beings, made in God's image (Genesis 1:27), owe him themselves. Caesar's claim ends where he claims what is God's, which is why the apostles later refused an order to stop preaching (Acts 5:29).

Against the Sadducees Jesus affirms the bodily resurrection from the Torah itself. God named himself the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob to Moses long after their deaths (Exodus 3:6), and he is not the God of the dead but of the living (verse 32). Resurrection life is not a copy of this life's arrangements, since the raised will not marry; it rests on the power of God and his faithfulness to those he has bound to himself by name.

Jesus sums up the Law in love for God with the whole person, from Deuteronomy 6:5, and love for the neighbor as oneself, from Leviticus 19:18, and says the second is like the first. These do not replace the commandments; the whole Law and the Prophets hang on them (verse 40), so every command is to be read as a form of this double love. Paul says the same when he calls love the fulfillment of the Law (Romans 13:8-10).

Jesus' question from Psalm 110:1 shows that the Messiah is more than a restored Davidic king: David, speaking by the Spirit, calls him Lord and hears God invite him to sit at his right hand. The apostles read the psalm as fulfilled when the risen Jesus was exalted to that place (Acts 2:34-36, Hebrews 1:13), and Jesus himself joins it to Daniel 7:13 at his trial (26:64).

words.note: Gamos, wedding, wedding feast. It occurs sixteen times in the New Testament, eight of them in this parable, where it runs like a refrain through verses 2 to 12, and again in the parable of the ten virgins (25:10). BDAG gives both the ceremony and the celebration, often in the plural as here, since a wedding meant days of feasting. Scripture pictures God's covenant with his people as a marriage (Isaiah 62:5, Hosea 2:19), Jesus calls himself the bridegroom (9:15), and the story ends with the wedding supper of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7-9). The feast in this parable is that one.

Klētos, called, invited. It occurs ten times in the New Testament in the critical text, only here in the Gospels; Paul uses it for believers as those ‘called to be saints’ (Romans 1:7, 1 Corinthians 1:2). Here it stands beside eklektos, chosen: the called are the many who receive the invitation (the related verb kaleō runs through verses 3 to 9), and the chosen are those who are found at the feast rightly clothed. The saying of verse 14 warns against presuming on an invitation; how it relates to God's electing grace is discussed under the hard question.

Enduma, garment, clothing; eight times in the New Testament, seven of them in Matthew. Elsewhere it is John's camel-hair garment (3:4), the clothing God provides (6:25, 6:28), the sheep's clothing of false prophets (7:15), and the angel's garment white as snow at the tomb (28:3). The phrase in verses 11 and 12, enduma gamou, is simply ‘wedding clothing’. The word itself does not decide whether the garment stands for imputed righteousness, charity, or a changed life; that comes from the story and from Matthew's wider teaching.

Eikōn, image, likeness. It occurs twenty-three times in the New Testament, only here in Matthew (verse 20). It is the word of the Greek Old Testament in Genesis 1:26-27, where God makes humanity according to his image. Jesus' question about whose image is on the coin invites his hearers to ask whose image they bear. Paul later calls Christ the image of God (2 Corinthians 4:4, Colossians 1:15) and speaks of believers being conformed to the image of the Son (Romans 8:29).

Apodidōmi, to give back, pay what is owed, render. It occurs about forty-eight times in the New Testament and is frequent in Matthew: of fulfilling vows to the Lord (5:33), of paying a debt to the last penny (5:26, 18:25-34), and of tenants who will give the fruits in their season (21:41). The questioners asked whether it was lawful to give (dounai) the tax; Jesus answers with the verb of repayment. The coin is already Caesar's, so returning it is a limited debt, while God's claim, stated in the same breath, is prior and total. It neither baptizes Rome's rule nor calls for revolt.

Anastasis, resurrection, literally a standing up again. It occurs forty-two times in the New Testament and four times in Matthew, all in this debate (verses 23, 28, 30, 31). It refers to the dead being raised bodily at the end of the age, a hope expressed in Daniel 12:2 and 2 Maccabees 7 and held by the Pharisees, not to the survival of the soul alone. Matthew's Gospel will end with the risen Jesus himself, and it has already told of bodies of the saints raised at his death (27:52-53).

Kremannumi (kremaō), to hang, to hang up. It occurs seven times in the New Testament, most often of hanging on a tree or cross (Acts 5:30, 10:39; Galatians 3:13), and of a millstone hung around the neck (18:6). In verse 40 the image is of everything suspended from a peg or a hinge: the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments. The Mishnah uses the same picture of rules that hang by a hair from a few verses (m. Hagigah 1:8); Jesus' two commands are the strong peg from which the whole Scripture hangs.

Kurios, lord, master, and in the Greek Old Testament the ordinary rendering of the divine name YHWH. It occurs more than seven hundred times in the New Testament. In verse 37 it translates the divine name of Deuteronomy 6:5; in verse 44 it stands twice in Psalm 110:1, once for YHWH and once for the Hebrew adoni, ‘my lord’, the address of an inferior to a superior. Jesus' question turns on the second: a father does not call his own descendant lord.

christ:
The chapter places Jesus at the center of each scene. In the parable the whole feast is given for the king's son, so that refusing the invitation is refusing him. The prophets had pictured God as Israel's husband (Isaiah 54:5, Hosea 2:19) and the age to come as a banquet on his mountain (Isaiah 25:6-8); Jesus has already called himself the bridegroom whose presence makes fasting impossible (9:15), and he will describe the kingdom again as a wedding for which the wise are ready (25:1-13). The servants sent and mistreated recall the prophets, and the tenants' parable just before it has told where that pattern leads: the son himself will be seized and killed (21:38-39). The invitation that then goes out to the roads is the one the risen Jesus sends at the end of the Gospel, to make disciples of all nations (28:19).

In the debates Jesus is the wise teacher who cannot be trapped, and more. He gives Caesar and God what belongs to each, and he himself, the true image of God, will give himself wholly to God. He answers the Sadducees from God's covenant name at the bush, and within days his own resurrection will be the first fruits of the life he defends (1 Corinthians 15:20). He sums up the Law in love for God and neighbor, and in the passion that follows he fulfills both, submitting to the Father's will in Gethsemane (26:39) and giving his life as a ransom for many (20:28).

Finally, he asks the question the whole Gospel has been answering. Matthew opened by calling Jesus ‘the son of David, the son of Abraham’ (1:1), and blind men, a Canaanite mother, and the Jerusalem crowd have hailed him as Son of David (9:27, 15:22, 21:9). Here he asks how David's son can be David's Lord. He leaves it unanswered, but he answers it himself at his trial: the high priest asks whether he is the Christ, the Son of God, and Jesus replies that they will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven (26:63-64), joining Psalm 110:1 to Daniel 7:13. Psalm 110:1 became the Old Testament text the New Testament cites or echoes more often than any other (Acts 2:34-36, 1 Corinthians 15:25, Hebrews 1:13). He is David's son by descent and David's Lord by right, and the church's confession that he is ‘seated at the right hand of the Father’ grows from this psalm.
interpretation:
The wedding garment has had a long reception. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 4.36.6, around 180) took it as the works of righteousness in which the called must be clothed so that the Spirit of God may rest on them. Augustine (Sermon 90) and Gregory the Great (Homilies on the Gospels 38, preached in Rome in the early 590s) both identified it as charity, and Gregory pictured it as a cloth woven between two beams, love of God and love of neighbor, tying the parable to the commandment later in this chapter. Calvin, in his Harmony of the Gospels (1555), judged the dispute whether the garment is faith or a holy life a useless controversy, since faith cannot be separated from good works nor good works come from anywhere but faith. Protestant preachers have often read it as the righteousness of Christ given to the believer (Isaiah 61:10), and Catholic readers as grace and charity. Johann Franck's Communion hymn Schmücke dich, o liebe Seele (1649), ‘Deck thyself, my soul, with gladness’, dresses the soul for the Lord's feast, and Bach built his cantata BWV 180 (Leipzig, 1724) on it for the Twentieth Sunday after Trinity, when Matthew 22:1-14 was the Gospel; his BWV 162 (Weimar, about 1715) and BWV 49 (1726) were written for the same Sunday.

The burning of the city in verse 7 was read from the fathers onward as the fall of Jerusalem, often as proof that God had rejected the Jewish people, a reading the Second Vatican Council's Nostra Aetate (1965) and many Protestant bodies have since repudiated. Modern parable study, from Joachim Jeremias's The Parables of Jesus to Amy-Jill Levine's Short Stories by Jesus (2014), has compared Matthew's version with Luke 14:15-24 and saying 64 of the Gospel of Thomas, and Levine has warned against reading Jesus' parables as allegories of Jewish failure.

The tax saying was cited by Justin Martyr (First Apology 17) to assure the emperor that Christians paid their taxes while worshiping God alone, and Tertullian (On Idolatry 15) drew the image argument still preached: give Caesar the coin that bears his image and give God yourself, since you bear his. Luther's Temporal Authority (1523) and Calvin's Institutes (4.20) built on it, and ‘render unto Caesar’, from the King James Version, became an English proverb. Titian's The Tribute Money (1516, Dresden) paints this scene; Masaccio's fresco of the same name in Florence shows a different story, the coin in the fish's mouth (17:24-27). Bach's Weimar cantata Nur jedem das Seine (BWV 163, 1715), ‘To each his own’, and his Leipzig cantatas BWV 139 (1724) and 52 (1726) were written for the Twenty-third Sunday after Trinity, when this passage was read.

The resurrection debate mattered to synagogue and church alike. The Mishnah excludes from the world to come anyone who says the resurrection of the dead is not taught in the Torah (m. Sanhedrin 10:1), and the Babylonian Talmud gathers rabbinic proofs of it from the Torah (b. Sanhedrin 90b-92a), among them Rabbi Simai's argument that God promised the land to the patriarchs themselves (Exodus 6:4), so they must live to receive it, close to the shape of Jesus' argument. The second blessing of the daily Amidah praises God who gives life to the dead.

The double commandment became a center of Christian ethics. The Didache (1:2) opens its way of life with love of God and neighbor, and Augustine (On Christian Doctrine 1.36.40) taught that anyone who thinks he understands the Scriptures but does not build up this double love has not yet understood them. Bach's BWV 96 (1724) and 169 (1726) were written for the Eighteenth Sunday after Trinity, when verses 34 to 46 were read. On Psalm 110, Justin Martyr reports Jewish teachers applying it to Hezekiah (Dialogue with Trypho 33, 83), the Talmud (b. Nedarim 32b) and Rashi read it of Abraham, and David Hay (Glory at the Right Hand, 1973) traced its uses in early Christianity. The Revised Common Lectionary reads the chapter in Year A on Propers 23 to 25, and the Roman lectionary on the Twenty-eighth to Thirtieth Sundays in Ordinary Time.
text:
English Bibles differ at several points in this chapter, mostly where the King James Version follows later manuscripts.

In verse 10 the manuscripts divide over the word for the place that was filled. Codex Sinaiticus, the first hand of Codex Vaticanus, and a few others read numphōn, ‘wedding hall’ or bridal chamber, which Westcott and Hort printed; most manuscripts read gamos, ‘wedding feast’, the word used everywhere else in the parable, which NA28 prints. The BSB's ‘wedding hall’ gives the sense of either. In verse 13 the King James Version adds ‘take him away’ between binding and casting out, from later manuscripts. In verse 30 the King James Version's ‘as the angels of God in heaven’ reflects manuscripts that add ‘of God’; the critical editions lack it. In verse 32 the King James Version's ‘God is not the God of the dead’ follows the Textus Receptus, where modern editions have ‘He is not the God of the dead’. In verse 44 the earliest manuscripts read ‘under your feet’ (hupokatō), while later ones read ‘your footstool’, the wording of the Greek Psalm, which the King James Version follows.

The quotation of Deuteronomy 6:5 in verse 37 has three terms, heart, soul, and mind (dianoia), where the Hebrew has heart, soul, and might, and Mark has four (Mark 12:30). Manuscripts of the Greek Old Testament differ between ‘heart’ and ‘mind’ for the first term, which may explain how ‘mind’ entered the saying. The saying of verse 14, ‘many are called, but few are chosen’, also appears in the King James Version at 20:16, where it was added in later manuscripts from this verse. Psalm 110 is Psalm 109 in the Greek and Latin numbering.

teach.big: The king's feast for his Son is open to everyone who will come, and the Son who issues the invitation claims the whole person, rising above every trap to show that God's image, God's life, God's love, and God's throne all belong to him.

outline.t: God's invitation is generous and persistent, and refusing it is refusing the Son; when the first guests will not come, the hall is filled from the roads with the evil and the good.
Grace invites everyone but does not leave a guest unchanged; the king himself inspects the hall, and an invitation presumed on is not a welcome received.
Jesus refuses both revolt and idolatry: give the ruler his coin, and give God what bears his image, which is all of you.
Doubt about the resurrection comes from knowing neither the Scriptures nor the power of God; the God who binds himself to his people by name does not abandon them to death.
The whole Law and the Prophets hang on love for God with the whole self and love for the neighbor as oneself, and every other command is read through them.
The Messiah is more than David's son; David calls him Lord, God seats him at his right hand, and every question about Jesus finally comes back to who he is.

teach.pitfalls:
The parable is often preached as proof that God rejected the Jewish people and replaced them with the church. The invited guests who kill the servants stand for leaders who reject God's messengers, as in the parable of the tenants just before it (21:45), and the first guests gathered into the new hall, the apostles and the Jerusalem church, were Jews. Verse 7 should not be used to present the destruction of Jerusalem as God's verdict on a people. A second misreading makes the wedding garment a dress code of respectability, as if the poor or the unwashed were unwelcome; the hall was filled from the streets, and the garment is the response the invitation calls for, not a social standard. A third turns ‘many are called, but few are chosen’ into a statistic about how many will be saved; it is a warning against presuming on an invitation.

The tax saying is often used to sort life into two compartments, the political owed to the state and the spiritual owed to God, or to demand unconditional obedience to government. Jesus' point is that everything belongs to God, Caesar included; the state's claim is real and limited. The Sadducee debate is sometimes used to teach that the dead become angels or that marriage has no meaning beyond this life. Jesus says the raised will be like the angels in not marrying, not that they become angels. Nor does his argument hang on the present tense of ‘I am’, since the Hebrew of Exodus 3:6 has no verb; it hangs on God's covenant faithfulness to the patriarchs. The great commandment is sometimes preached as a command to love yourself first; the text assumes self-love and commands love of the neighbor. And Psalm 110 is sometimes taught as if Jesus denied being David's son; he asks how both can be true.
teach.pastoral: The chapter presses on several people in the room. Widows and widowers, and anyone who has buried a spouse, may hear verse 30 as a threat that their love will be erased. Teach it as Jesus meant it: marriage in this age is bound up with death and the need for heirs, and the God of the living keeps hold of those he names; the promise is fuller life, not lesser love. The anxious and scrupulous may hear the wedding garment as a trap, wondering whether they are secretly the guest without clothes. The man in the story is not someone troubled about his standing but someone who came as though the king's son did not matter, and who had nothing to say. Those who fear they are not worthy are the very people the king sent his servants to find. Believers who have suffered under oppressive governments, or who come from countries where paying Caesar meant compromise, need to hear that Jesus' answer limits the state as much as it honors it.

hard.q: Why is the man without wedding clothes thrown out, when the guests were gathered off the streets with no warning, and what does ‘few are chosen’ mean?
hard.a:
The objection is sharp. The king's servants gather everyone they can find, ‘both evil and good’, straight from the roads; then the king throws one of them into the outer darkness for what he is wearing. On its face this looks arbitrary, even cruel, a reversal of the generosity that filled the hall. The closing saying seems to make matters worse, since ‘many are called, but few are chosen’ can sound like a decree that most who hear the invitation are excluded in advance. Skeptical readers have taken the scene as an example of the Gospel's harsh judgment sayings, and Jewish readers, among them Amy-Jill Levine (Short Stories by Jesus, 2014), have pressed Christians to notice how parables like this one were used to cast Jews as the refusing guests. Within the church, Calvinist and Arminian readers have argued over whether verse 14 teaches unconditional election or human response.

Several answers are offered. Some interpreters propose that the host supplied festal garments, citing Jehu's provision of vestments in 2 Kings 10:22, so that the man had refused what was given; there is no firm evidence of such a custom at weddings, and the reading should be held loosely. More weight falls on the story itself. The man is addressed as ‘Friend’ and given the chance to answer, and he is speechless: he has no excuse, which implies he could have come ready. The nearest Jewish parallel, Yohanan ben Zakkai's parable of the king whose servants had to be dressed and waiting (b. Shabbat 153a), makes the garment a picture of readiness, and Zephaniah 1:7-8 links God's consecrated guests with proper clothing. From there interpreters diverge. Irenaeus saw the garment as works of righteousness and the Spirit; Augustine and Gregory the Great as charity; many Protestants, following Isaiah 61:10, as the righteousness God gives; and many others, noting Matthew's steady stress on doing the Father's will (7:21, 25:31-46), as the fruit of repentance. Calvin held that faith and good works cannot be separated here, and many readers today hold both together: grace invites everyone, and grace does not leave a guest unchanged.

On verse 14, Reformed interpreters read the chosen as those God has elected, whose election shows in their response; Arminian, Wesleyan, and many Catholic and Orthodox readers take ‘chosen’ as describing those who accept the invitation and are found fit, so that the saying warns against presuming on a call. Fourth Ezra, a Jewish apocalypse from around AD 100, has a similar saying, that many have been created but few will be saved (4 Ezra 8:3). Christians differ on how election and response relate, a second-order question. The parable's own point is not to calculate how many but to warn those already in the hall.

hard.q: Did Jesus approve of paying taxes to Rome, or was his answer a clever refusal?
hard.a:
The traditional reading, that Jesus endorsed paying the tax while reserving worship for God, has been challenged from several directions. S. G. F. Brandon (Jesus and the Zealots, 1967) argued that any devout Jew knew that Israel's land and everything in it belonged to God alone, so ‘give to God what is God's’ left nothing for Caesar; on his view the saying was a veiled refusal that the Gospels later softened into loyalty to Rome. Richard Horsley (Jesus and the Spiral of Violence, 1987), who did not share Brandon's picture of an armed Jesus, still read the saying in the setting of popular resistance to Roman exploitation, and others have heard irony in it: the questioners who carry Caesar's image into the temple courts may as well give it back to him. Luke reports that Jesus was accused before Pilate of forbidding payment of tribute (Luke 23:2), which some take as evidence that his words could be heard that way. From the other side, many Christians have used the saying to require near-unconditional obedience to the state.

The responses start with the exchange itself. Jesus asks for the coin, has his questioners name the image and inscription, and tells them to ‘give back’ (apodote) what is Caesar's, the language of repaying a debt. That concedes a real obligation. But he adds at once that God's things belong to God, and the coin's image invites the obvious question of what bears God's image. Justin Martyr (First Apology 17) and Tertullian (On Idolatry 15) read it as both loyalty and limit, and Paul's teaching on paying taxes to whom taxes are due (Romans 13:6-7) stands close to it. The limit is equally real: when rulers forbade the apostles to preach, they answered that they must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29), and the Barmen Declaration (1934), written by German Protestants resisting the Nazi church policy, appealed to Christ's lordship over every sphere of life. Luther's two kingdoms, Calvin's teaching on civil government (Institutes 4.20), Anabaptist nonresistance, and Catholic social teaching all develop the saying differently. What the text will not support is either a Zealot's refusal or a state's claim to the whole person.

observe: How many times does the king send his servants in verses 3 to 9, and how does each group of invited guests respond?
What exactly do the Pharisees' disciples and the Herodians say about Jesus in verse 16 before they ask their question, and how does he answer?
Which two Old Testament commands does Jesus quote in verses 37 to 39, and what does he say depends on them?
interpret: What do you think the wedding garment represents, and why do you think the man was speechless when the king asked about it?
Why does Jesus answer the Sadducees from the words God spoke at the burning bush, and what does it mean that God is the God of the living?
Why does it matter that David, speaking by the Spirit, calls his descendant ‘Lord’? What does the question reveal about who the Messiah is?
apply: The first guests went off to a field and a business. What ordinary good things crowd out God's invitation for you?
If you bear God's image, what would it look like for him to claim all of you, including what you owe to the government and to others?
Which of the two great commandments do you find harder to keep this week, and what would it look like to let the other one hang on it?
